--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Network Diagrams and Activity-on-Node (AON) ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Build** an activity-on-node (AON) network from a precedence table. 2. **Apply** the rules for constructing a valid network diagram. 3. **Perform** the forward pass to find early start (ES) and early finish (EF). 4. **Perform** the backward pass to find late start (LS) and late finish (LF). 5. **Calculate** total float and identify the **critical path**. 6. **Compute** a three-point (PERT) activity duration. 7. **Choose** a strategy to shorten the critical path when the project is too long.
Before we begin: which task can slip without moving the deadline? On any project some tasks have slack and some do not. Guessing wrong --- pouring effort into a task with float while a zero-float task quietly slips --- is one of the most common ways schedules die. The network diagram tells you which is which.
## Introduction: when can we launch? The RC-vehicle WBS gives you a list of activities and their durations. It does *not* tell you how long the whole project takes, because the activities are not all independent --- you cannot assemble a prototype before the body is designed. A **network diagram** captures those dependencies and answers the question the sponsor actually cares about: **what is the earliest the project can finish, and which activities decide that date?** ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** Every automotive program plan is a critical-path network: the "job one" date is the length of the longest dependent chain. A food-plant commissioning schedule uses the same math to decide whether sanitation qualification can overlap controls checkout. A defense contractor reports critical-path status to the customer monthly --- slipping a critical task is a contractual event. :::
## From WBS to precedence table For each activity you need its **duration** and its **immediate predecessors** --- the activities that must finish before it can start. Rules for a valid AON network: 1. Determine precedence ordering **before** drawing. 2. Networks flow **left to right**. 3. An activity cannot begin until **all** connected predecessors are complete. 4. Arrows show **precedence and logical flow** (they may cross, but minimize it). 5. Every activity has a **unique identifier**. 6. **No looping** back to an earlier activity. 7. It is common (not required) to start from a **single start node**... 8. ...and end at a **single end node**. ## AON node anatomy Each activity is a box with six numbers: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The six-number activity node. Forward pass fills the top row (ES, DUR, EF); backward pass fills the bottom (LS, FLT, LF).](06-Network-Diagrams-and-AON_files/figure-html/fig-node-anatomy-06-1.png){#fig-node-anatomy-06 fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: An activity with 2+ predecessors flowing **in** is a **merge**; one with 2+ successors flowing **out** is a **burst**. ## Worked Example: the RC-vehicle sub-project network Ten activities (a simplified slice of the project): ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Activity Duration (days) Predecessors
A 5
B 8 A
C 3 B
D 4 A
E 5 C
F 7 C
G 6 D,E
H 8 F
I 6 G
J 5 H,I
````` ::: ::: ### Forward pass (ES, EF) Move left to right. $EF = ES + DUR$. Carry each EF forward as the successor's ES --- **except at a merge, where the ES is the largest incoming EF.** ### Backward pass (LS, LF) Move right to left from the project finish. $LS = LF - DUR$. Carry each LS back as the predecessor's LF --- **except at a burst, where the LF is the smallest outgoing LS.** ### Float and the critical path $$FLT = LS - ES = LF - EF$$ Activities with **zero float** cannot slip without delaying the whole project --- together they form the **critical path**. Live cell --- a base-R critical-path solver. Run it, then change a duration or a predecessor in `acts` and watch the project duration and the critical path move. ```{webr-r} #| label: cpm-solve-06 # The ten activities: id, duration, and comma-separated predecessors. acts <- data.frame( id = LETTERS[1:10], dur = c(5, 8, 3, 4, 5, 7, 6, 8, 6, 5), pred = c("", "A", "B", "A", "C", "C", "D,E", "F", "G", "H,I"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # A small critical-path solver (base R only). cpm <- function(df) { df$pred <- strsplit(df$pred, ",") n <- nrow(df); id <- df$id ES <- EF <- LS <- LF <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, n), id) # Forward pass (ids are already in a valid topological order here) for (i in seq_len(n)) { p <- df$pred[[i]]; p <- p[p != ""] ES[i] <- if (length(p) == 0) 0 else max(EF[p]) EF[i] <- ES[i] + df$dur[i] } proj <- max(EF) # Backward pass for (i in rev(seq_len(n))) { succ <- id[sapply(df$pred, function(pp) id[i] %in% pp)] LF[i] <- if (length(succ) == 0) proj else min(LS[succ]) LS[i] <- LF[i] - df$dur[i] } data.frame(Activity = id, Dur = df$dur, ES = ES, EF = EF, LS = LS, LF = LF, Float = LS - ES, Critical = ifelse(LS - ES == 0, " <- critical", "")) } res <- cpm(acts) print(res, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nProject duration: %d days\n", max(res$EF))) cat("Critical path:", paste(res$Activity[res$Float == 0], collapse = " - "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Total float per activity. The zero-float bars (A, B, C, E, G, I, J) are the critical path; D has 12 days of slack, F and H have 2.](06-Network-Diagrams-and-AON_files/figure-html/fig-cpm-float-06-1.png){#fig-cpm-float-06 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: The whole forward/backward/float sequence is one connected calculation --- change any duration and every downstream number moves --- so work it as a block, not as isolated steps. ## Three-point (PERT) duration estimates When a duration is uncertain, estimate three values --- **optimistic** $o$, **most likely** $m$, **pessimistic** $p$ --- and combine them: $$t_e = \frac{o + 4m + p}{6}$$ ### Try it yourself: PERT durations ```{webr-r} #| label: pert-te-06 tasks <- data.frame( id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"), o = c(12, 7, 15, 9, 24), m = c(15, 10, 19, 13, 26), p = c(17, 13, 23, 16, 30) ) tasks$te <- round((tasks$o + 4 * tasks$m + tasks$p) / 6, 2) tasks$sd <- round((tasks$p - tasks$o) / 6, 2) # activity standard deviation print(tasks, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nSum of expected durations along this chain: %.2f days\n", sum(tasks$te))) ```
Why the weight of 4 on the most-likely value? PERT assumes each activity duration follows a Beta distribution skewed toward the most-likely value, with the optimistic and pessimistic values as the tails. Weighting $m$ by 4 and $o$, $p$ by 1 each (dividing by 6) is the standard approximation of that distribution's mean. The activity standard deviation $(p - o)/6$ becomes important in [Chapter 8](08-Project-Scheduling.qmd), where you combine them to find the probability of finishing on time.
## Shortening the critical path Only work on the **critical path** shortens the project. Options, roughly in order of preference: 1. **Eliminate** critical tasks (is it truly needed?). 2. **Re-plan series paths to run in parallel.** 3. **Overlap** sequential tasks (start the successor before the predecessor fully finishes --- *fast-tracking*). 4. **Shorten durations on critical activities** --- prefer earlier-starting tasks, then the longest, then the easiest, then the ones **cheapest to speed up**. ### Try it yourself: recompute the critical path after a change ```{webr-r} #| label: path-duration-06 # All start-to-finish paths through the sub-project network, with activity durations. dur <- c(A = 5, B = 8, C = 3, D = 4, E = 5, F = 7, G = 6, H = 8, I = 6, J = 5) paths <- list( "A-B-C-E-G-I-J" = c("A","B","C","E","G","I","J"), "A-B-C-F-H-J" = c("A","B","C","F","H","J"), "A-D-G-I-J" = c("A","D","G","I","J") ) path_len <- sapply(paths, function(p) sum(dur[p])) cat("Baseline path lengths:\n"); print(path_len) cat(sprintf("Critical path: %s (%d days)\n\n", names(which.max(path_len)), max(path_len))) # Now crash B from 8 to 5 days and re-check: dur["B"] <- 5 path_len2 <- sapply(paths, function(p) sum(dur[p])) cat("After crashing B by 3 days:\n"); print(path_len2) cat(sprintf("New critical path: %s (%d days)\n", names(which.max(path_len2)), max(path_len2))) cat("Note how the critical path can *shift* to a different chain once you crash enough.\n") ``` ## The downside of network diagrams - Often **not drawn to scale** --- time is just a number, which can create a false sense of how much time is available. - Can be **too large and complex** to be useful. - **Faulty construction logic** can oversimplify or misrepresent the work. - Sometimes used for work they do not suit. - **Positive bias** creeps into PERT estimates (people are optimistic). ## Key Takeaways - Build the **AON network** from a precedence table (durations + immediate predecessors); it flows left to right with no loops. - **Forward pass**: $EF = ES + DUR$; at a **merge**, ES = the largest incoming EF. Gives the **project duration**. - **Backward pass**: $LS = LF - DUR$; at a **burst**, LF = the smallest outgoing LS. - **Float** $= LS - ES = LF - EF$. **Zero-float** activities form the **critical path** --- the longest dependent chain, and the only one worth shortening. - **PERT**: $t_e = (o + 4m + p)/6$, activity SD $= (p - o)/6$. - Shorten the critical path by **eliminating, parallelizing, overlapping, or crashing** critical tasks --- and re-check, because the critical path can shift. ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 6 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 6: The network comes together"} Daniel Cho has been asking the same question in every steering call since the charter was signed: when does the Trailblazer prototype actually ship to Kestrel? This week you have a real answer, because you and Priya Nandakumar finally turned the "Prototype Build & Qualification" branch of the WBS into an activity-on-node network instead of a list of jobs on a whiteboard. Ten activities, in the sequence the tooling, procurement, and testing work actually has to happen: concept CAD and detailed design release feed three parallel branches --- Priya's body and frame tooling builds, and Marcus Webb's motor-and-controller procurement from MCS --- which all have to finish before Sofia Reyes's team can assemble a prototype to test and certify. You run the forward pass first, activity by activity, and the merge at Prototype Assembly (F) is the one that matters: it cannot start until the *slowest* of tooling and procurement finishes, not the fastest. Motor and controller procurement (E) turns out to be the long pole at 25 days, arriving at the merge two full weeks after Marcus's frame tooling and five days after Priya's body tooling --- which is exactly why the MCS relationship is worth protecting rather than swapping out on price alone. The backward pass confirms it: activities A, B, E, F, H, I, and J all land with zero float. That chain --- concept CAD through detailed design, motor procurement, assembly, toy-safety certification, packaging, and your sign-off report to Renata Ford --- is the critical path, and it sets the whole prototype phase at 67 working days, just under 13.5 weeks. Body tooling (C) has 5 days of cushion, frame tooling (D) has 10, and the durability test (G) has 7 --- comfortable float today, but float that Priya and Sofia will need to manage carefully once resource assignments get made in a few weeks. You flag one thing for the team before the meeting ends: activity E is both the longest single activity on the critical path and completely outside Meridian's control once the purchase order is placed. Anything that slows MCS down slows the whole project down. That single line in the network diagram is the reason procurement risk is going to dominate next week's risk-identification session. | Activity | Description | Duration (days) | Predecessors | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | A | Concept CAD | 10 | --- | 0 | 10 | 0 | 10 | 0 | | B | Detailed design release | 8 | A | 10 | 18 | 10 | 18 | 0 | | C | Body tooling build | 20 | B | 18 | 38 | 23 | 43 | 5 | | D | Frame tooling build | 15 | B | 18 | 33 | 28 | 43 | 10 | | E | Motor & controls procurement (MCS) | 25 | B | 18 | 43 | 18 | 43 | 0 | | F | Prototype assembly | 6 | C, D, E | 43 | 49 | 43 | 49 | 0 | | G | Drop/durability test | 5 | F | 49 | 54 | 51 | 56 | 7 | | H | Toy-safety certification | 12 | F | 49 | 61 | 49 | 61 | 0 | | I | Packaging & client sample ship | 4 | G, H | 61 | 65 | 61 | 65 | 0 | | J | PM sign-off / report to Kestrel | 2 | I | 65 | 67 | 65 | 67 | 0 | : The Week 6 Meridian Trailblazer CPM network. Project duration: 67 working days. ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Solve this network | Activity | Predecessors | Duration | |---|---|---| | A | none | 3 | | B | A | 4 | | C | A | 2 | | D | B | 5 | | E | C | 1 | | F | E | 2 | | G | D, E | 4 | | H | F, G | 3 | | I | H | 6 | Find the project duration and the critical path. **Solution.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- data.frame( id = LETTERS[1:9], dur = c(3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 6), pred = c("", "A", "A", "B", "C", "E", "D,E", "F,G", "H"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) r1 <- cpm(p1) # reuse the solver defined earlier in this chapter print(r1, row.names = FALSE) cat(sprintf("\nProject duration: %d days\n", max(r1$EF))) cat("Critical path:", paste(r1$Activity[r1$Float == 0], collapse = " - "), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Activity Dur ES EF LS LF Float Critical A 3 0 3 0 3 0 <- critical B 4 3 7 3 7 0 <- critical C 2 3 5 9 11 6 D 5 7 12 7 12 0 <- critical E 1 5 6 11 12 6 F 2 6 8 14 16 8 G 4 12 16 12 16 0 <- critical H 3 16 19 16 19 0 <- critical I 6 19 25 19 25 0 <- critical Project duration: 25 days Critical path: A - B - D - G - H - I ``` ::: ::: Duration 25 days; critical path A--B--D--G--H--I. (The chain A--B--D--G is what pushes E, F, and C off the critical path --- D's 5 days arriving at the G merge beat E's early finish by 6 days.)
Problem 2: PERT and the optimistic tail An activity is estimated at $o = 6$, $m = 9$, $p = 24$ days. (a) What is $t_e$? (b) Why is $t_e$ noticeably larger than $m$? (c) What is the activity standard deviation? **Solution.** (a) $t_e = (6 + 36 + 24)/6 = 11$ days. (b) The pessimistic tail is far from the most-likely value (24 vs 9) while the optimistic tail is close (6 vs 9), so the distribution is **right-skewed** and its mean sits above $m$. (c) SD $= (24 - 6)/6 = 3$ days --- a wide, risky activity.
Problem 3 (discussion): which task do you crash? On the sub-project network, the critical path is A--B--C--E--G--I--J (38 days) and the sponsor needs 34. Crash data: B costs \$500/day to shorten (max 3 days), G costs \$1 200/day (max 2 days), E costs \$300/day (max 2 days). Which combination gets you to 34 days at least cost, and what do you check afterward? **Discussion points.** You need 4 days. Cheapest first: E for 2 days (\$600), then B for 2 days (\$1 000) --- total \$1 600 for 4 days. Avoid G at \$1 200/day. **Then re-run the network**: after removing 4 days from this chain, another path (e.g. A--B--C--F--H--J) may now be critical or co-critical, and crashing further would have to shorten *both*.
